name: Confucianism
summary: Confucianism holds that social and political order comes from moral self-cultivation, with a virtuous ruler leading by example and worthy, learned officials assisting him. It roots virtue in the family and filial piety, sees society as reciprocal role duties, and prefers ritual and moral formation to law and punishment. Heaven's mandate rests on securing the people's welfare, and Mencius and Xunzi both accept the removal of a tyrant.
scope: A canonical-core entry, not a family: the Analects, Mencius, Xunzi, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, read with the SEP and IEP accounts of their political implications. A position counts only where Confucius, Mencius and Xunzi (or the texts that speak to it) agree; where they differ it is a split. Neo-Confucianism, New Confucianism, dynastic state Confucianism and modern political Confucians are other subjects and are excluded, so no record of imperial regimes is used. Modern questions the classics never address are null.

missingStatements.text: Rulers and officials should be chosen for virtue and ability, not birth.
missingStatements.rationale: Analects 2.19 and 13.2, Mencius 2A5 and Xunzi IX all tell the ruler to advance the worthy and able and set aside the unfit, whatever their descent.

missingStatements.text: A government should first secure the people's livelihood and then educate them in morals.
missingStatements.rationale: Analects 13.9 says to enrich the people and then teach them, and Mencius 1A7 and 3A3 say the people without a settled livelihood lack a settled heart.

missingStatements.text: Social life should be ordered by fixed rules of ritual propriety that mark each person's rank and duties.
missingStatements.rationale: Analects 12.11 and 8.2 and Xunzi XIX make ritual propriety and role distinctions the basis of order.

notes: Searched every theme; most modern statements are null because the classics are silent. Xunzi alone says the state needs punishments for the unreformable and rejects replacement of rulers by the people at will (IEP), so consent answers are low. Mencius-only positions (well-field land system, tax rates, ministers' right to dethrone) are used only where Xunzi or the Analects agree. Many lines will have wide error bars; failure of the uncertainty rule would be an honest result. Citations of Mencius use the standard Book/part number (e.g. 1B8), identified from the Legge text on Wikisource; Xunzi citations use Dubs's book numbers.
